system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker MUT_STAG2 (damaging STAG2 mutation).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking: The STAG1 dependency in the STAG2-mutant lines looks like the known paralog synthetic lethality, since the two are cohesin paralogs. That fits, so I'll register it and replicate, and I only need one candidate, so I'll keep just STAG1.

input.mechanism: STAG1 and STAG2 are paralogous cohesin subunits that are mutually redundant in holding sister chromatids and maintaining cohesion/genome organization. STAG2 loss-of-function lines rely on STAG1 as the remaining cohesin-STAG subunit, so STAG1 knockout is selectively lethal in STAG2-mutant cells (synthetic lethality via paralog buffering loss). STAG1 is not broadly essential in the discovery set (mean effect in other lines -0.15), supporting a therapeutic window.

findings.claim: Cancer lines with damaging STAG2 mutation are selectively dependent on STAG1 (paralogous cohesin subunit); STAG1 knockout effect is about -0.58 in STAG2-mutant vs -0.15 in other lines in discovery, and replicated in held-out Broad lines (beta -0.53, p=7e-15, n=15 altered) and independent Sanger screens (beta -0.69, p=9e-13, n=8 altered). STAG1 is not broadly essential, supporting a window.

input.summary: Best candidate target for MUT_STAG2 cancers is STAG1. In discovery (626 lines, 17 STAG2-mutant), STAG1 was the top selective dependency (lineage-adjusted t=-6.2, q=1.5e-5), and no other gene came close. The signal is not driven by one lineage: it holds after leaving out each major lineage (Lymphoid, Bone, CNS, Bladder), and about 41% of altered lines are strongly STAG1-dependent versus 6% of others. STAG1 is not broadly essential. The biology fits paralog buffering: STAG1 and STAG2 are mutually redundant cohesin subunits, so STAG2-deficient cells rely on STAG1. The hypothesis was pre-registered and replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=7e-15) and independent Sanger screens (p=9e-13). Caveats: only 17 discovery lines carry the mutation, the effect is moderate (about 0.4 gene-effect units), and the mechanism is known from prior work on STAG2/STAG1 synthetic lethality, so the novelty is limited even though the data support it. Other associations (e.g., SNRNP35, RPL36AL) are broadly essential and offer no therapeutic window.
